usage: the plain, neutral noun for a male person
noun + 이에요/예요; 남자 ends in a vowel, so the contracted 예요
남자 used as a modifier in front of another noun, no particle needed
with a space it is a friend who happens to be male; 남자친구 written solid means boyfriend
examples: 저 사람은 남자예요.
That person is a man.
the simplest A는 B예요 identity sentence
남자 화장실은 2층에 있어요.
The men's restroom is on the second floor.
남자 glued to 화장실 acts like an adjective 'men's'
키 큰 남자가 우리 오빠예요.
The tall man is my older brother.
real situation: a modifier clause 키 큰 plus subject 남자가
nuance: 남자 (Sino-Korean 男子, literally 'male-person') is the flat, everyday noun for a man or male, with no warmth or rudeness built in — it simply states the category, the way 'male' does on a form. Its mirror word is 여자 (woman), and the dividing line you must keep straight is 남자 = any male in general versus 남편 (husband, 男便) = the specific man a woman is married to; an English speaker who reaches for 'my man' and says 내 남자 sounds like a song lyric, not 'my husband'. As a noun it takes 이에요/예요 and the subject marker 가 because it ends in a vowel (남자예요, 남자가), and it loves to sit in front of other nouns with no particle at all: 남자 화장실, 남자 옷, 남자 목소리. The notorious trap is spacing — 남자 친구 with a space is just a friend who is male, while 남자친구 squeezed into one word is a romantic boyfriend, so a stray space can change your whole sentence.

usage: the plain, neutral noun for a female person
noun + 예요 because 여자 ends in a vowel
여자 used as a modifier before another noun
with a space, a friend who is female; 여자친구 solid means girlfriend
examples: 저 사람은 여자예요.
That person is a woman.
the basic identity pattern A는 B예요
여자 옷 가게가 1층에 있어요.
The women's clothing store is on the first floor.
여자 stacked in front of 옷 to mean 'women's'
빨간 옷을 입은 여자가 제 친구예요.

real situation: a modifier clause describing which 여자

usage: a fully grown person; also one's elders
noun + 이에요 after the final consonant ㄴ
subject marker 이 because 어른 ends in a consonant
plural with 들, often the seniors you must respect
examples: 저는 이제 어른이에요.
I am an adult now.
어른 + 이에요 after the consonant ㄴ
어른한테는 존댓말을 써요.
We use polite speech to adults/elders.
everyday: shows the respect sense, 어른 = elder
어른들이 아이를 도와줬어요.
The grown-ups helped the child.
real situation: 어른 contrasted directly with 아이 (child)
nuance: 어른 is a native Korean word (no hanja) that covers two linked ideas: an adult as opposed to 아이 (child), and, just as importantly, one's elders — the older people a Korean is socially obliged to treat with respect. That second sense is where English speakers slip: 'adult' in English is a neutral age category, but 어른 often means 'a senior I must bow and use 존댓말 to', so 어른을 공경하다 (respect your elders) is a core phrase. Compare it with three neighbors — 성인 (成人, the legal/clinical 'adult' on documents and age ratings, e.g. 성인 영화), 노인 (an elderly person), and 아이 (child): 어른 is the warm, relational everyday word, 성인 is the bureaucratic one. It ends in the consonant ㄴ, so it takes 이에요 and 이 (어른이에요, 어른이). The adjective 어른스럽다 (to be mature, grown-up in manner) is built straight from it.

usage: a very young child; also a term of endearment
noun + 예요 because 아기 ends in a vowel
subject marker 가 after a vowel
아기 modifying 옷 with no particle
examples: 아기가 자요.
The baby is sleeping.
simplest 아기 + 가 + verb
아기가 정말 귀여워요.
The baby is really cute.
everyday: pairs with the adjective 귀엽다
우리 아기는 지금 돌이에요.
Our baby is one year old now.
real situation: 돌 = first birthday; 우리 아기 as endearment

The boundary to hold: 아기 is roughly 'baby/infant' (newborn up to toddler), 아이 covers any child up through about pre-teen, and 어린이 (children) is the formal/institutional word you see on signs (어린이 보호구역 = school zone). In casual speech 아기 is very often softened to 애기, and shortened further to 애 in fast talk, though 아기 is the textbook spelling. The endearment use matters culturally: parents say 우리 아기 ('our baby') even to a grown child the way English speakers say 'my baby'. Because it ends in a vowel it takes 예요 and 가 (아기예요, 아기가), and as a modifier it needs no particle: 아기 옷, 아기 침대, 아기 손.

usage: a young adult, roughly in their 20s-30s
noun + 이에요 after the consonant ㄴ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
common policy/news collocation; also 청년 일자리 (youth jobs)
examples: 저 청년은 아주 성실해요.
That young man is very diligent.
청년 + 은 as topic; here it leans toward a young man
요즘 청년들이 취업 때문에 힘들어요.
These days young people struggle because of finding jobs.
everyday: 청년들 as a social group in the news
정부가 청년 일자리 정책을 발표했어요.
The government announced a youth-jobs policy.
real situation: the bureaucratic register 청년 lives in

Mind two boundaries: a teenager is 청소년 (靑少年, adolescent), not 청년, and a literal child is 아이/어린이; 청년 starts after the teens. It can specifically evoke a young man (as in older praise like 참 좋은 청년 = 'a fine young man'), but in modern policy language it covers young people of any gender. Ending in ㄴ, it takes 이에요 and 이 (청년이에요, 청년이).

usage: an old person; neutral in writing, blunt to the face
noun + 이에요 after the consonant ㄴ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
policy collocation; also 노인 인구 (elderly population)
examples: 그 노인은 공원에서 운동해요.
That elderly person exercises in the park.
노인 + 은 as topic, third-person description
버스에서 어르신께 자리를 양보했어요.
I gave up my seat to an elderly person on the bus.
everyday: note the POLITE 어르신, not 노인, when showing respect
우리나라는 노인 인구가 빠르게 늘고 있어요.
Our country's elderly population is growing fast.
real situation: 노인 in its neutral statistical/news sense
nuance: 노인 (Sino-Korean 老人, literally 'old-person') is the standard, neutral word for an elderly person in writing and statistics — 노인 복지 (elderly welfare), 노인 인구 (elderly population), 노인정 (senior center). The critical register catch for English speakers: 노인 is fine on paper but feels blunt, even cold, when used to or about a specific older person in front of them; the respectful word is 어르신, which adds deference the way 'esteemed elder' would. So you describe the demographic as 노인 but address grandma's friend as 어르신. Distinguish it from 어른 (an adult / one's elder, any grown person) and 할아버지·할머니 (grandfather/grandmother, also used warmly for unrelated old people). Ending in ㄴ, it takes 이에요 and 이 (노인이에요, 노인이). Default to 어르신 whenever politeness or face-to-face contact is involved.

usage: the person who owns something or runs a place
noun + 이에요 after the consonant ㄴ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
집 (house) + 주인, written solid as one word
examples: 이 가게 주인이 친절해요.
The owner of this shop is kind.
가게 주인 = shop owner, simple A 주인 pattern
이 가방 주인이 누구예요?
Who is the owner of this bag?
everyday: asking whose something is, 주인 + 이
집주인한테 보증금을 돌려받았어요.
I got the deposit back from the landlord.
real situation: 집주인 + 한테, the rental context

The combination you must know is 집 + 주인 → 집주인, the standard word for a landlord, written solid as one word; leaving a space (집 주인) reads literally as 'the owner of the house' and feels off for the rental sense. usage: a husband and wife together as a unit
noun + 예요 because 부부 ends in a vowel
subject marker 가 after a vowel
신혼 (new marriage) + 부부, one word; cf. 노부부 (elderly couple)
examples: 저 두 분은 부부예요.
Those two people are a married couple.
부부 + 예요; 두 분 is the polite counter for people
그 부부가 카페를 같이 운영해요.
That couple runs a cafe together.
everyday: a married pair doing something jointly
신혼부부가 새 아파트로 이사했어요.
The newlyweds moved into a new apartment.
real situation: the set word 신혼부부
nuance: 부부 (Sino-Korean 夫婦, literally 'husband-wife') means specifically a married couple — the husband and wife taken together as one social unit. The boundary English speakers must respect is 부부 (married) versus 커플 (a loanword from 'couple', a dating pair who may not be married at all); calling your boyfriend-and-yourself 부부 implies you are actually married. It is a dignified, neutral word that combines readily: 신혼부부 (newlyweds), 노부부 (an elderly couple), 잉꼬부부 (a lovebird couple who get along beautifully), 부부 싸움 (a marital spat). Because it ends in a vowel it takes 예요 and 가 (부부예요, 부부가). One more nuance: 부부 names the relationship/unit, not the individuals, so you don't use it to point at one person — for that you'd say 남편 (husband) or 아내 (wife).

usage: refers back to the very person being discussed
noun + 이에요 after the consonant ㄴ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
ubiquitous on forms; also 본인 서명 (one's own signature)
examples: 본인이 직접 오셔야 해요.
The person must come in person.
본인 + 이; classic counter/office phrasing
여기에 본인 이름을 쓰세요.
Write your own name here.
everyday: 본인 modifying 이름 = 'your own'
이 일은 본인만 결정할 수 있어요.
Only the person themselves can decide this.
real situation: 본인 + 만 = 'only oneself'
nuance: 본인 (Sino-Korean 本人, literally 'origin/root-person', i.e. the actual person concerned) is a formal-leaning word meaning 'oneself' or 'the very person in question'. Its natural home is officialdom — counters, banks, forms, hospitals: 본인 확인 (identity check), 본인 서명 (sign it yourself), 본인 부담금 (the portion the patient pays). The trap for English speakers is two-fold. First, register: in friendly conversation 본인 sounds stiff and bureaucratic, so for 'myself' say 저/나 and for 'yourself' use the person's name or title — overusing 본인 with friends is like saying 'the undersigned' at a coffee shop. Second, reference: 본인 always points back to the relevant person, not necessarily the speaker, so 본인이 오세요 means 'have the person themselves come', whereas to volunteer yourself you'd say 제가 갈게요. usage: an unspecified, unknown person (a statement word)
누군가 + 가; the subject marker is commonly added
누군가 + 를 as the object of a verb
누군가 + 에게, the person something is directed to

Someone is outside.
누군가 can stand bare before 있어요
누군가가 문을 두드렸어요.
Someone knocked on the door.

It is built from 누구 ('who') plus the bound 가, and the single most important fact about it is that, unlike bare 누구, it is a STATEMENT word, not a question; 누군가 왔어요 is 'someone came', never 'who came?'. 아무 + 도; always paired with a NEGATIVE verb
아무 + 나; 'anyone will do', with a positive verb
아무 + 데 (place) + 나; cf. 아무거나 (anything), 아무 때나 (anytime)

아무도 with the negative 없어요 = 'nobody'
이건 아무나 할 수 있어요.
Anyone can do this.
everyday: 아무나 + positive = 'anyone at all'
아무 말도 하지 마세요.
Don't say anything.

So the polarity of the verb must match the particle: 도 ↔ negative, 나 ↔ positive. Memorize the family as fixed sets — 아무도 (nobody), 아무나 (anybody), 아무것도/아무거나 (nothing/anything), 아무 데도/아무 데나 (nowhere/anywhere), 아무 때나 (anytime). usage: an adult/older man; also a way to address one
noun + 예요 because 아저씨 ends in a vowel
subject marker 가 after a vowel
calling out to a male worker, driver, or older man
examples: 저 아저씨가 길을 알려 줬어요.
That man showed me the way.
아저씨 + 가, describing an older man
아저씨, 이거 얼마예요?
Mister, how much is this?
everyday: 아저씨 as a direct form of address to a vendor
택시 아저씨가 아주 친절하셨어요.
The taxi driver was very kind.
real situation: 택시 아저씨 = the (male) taxi driver
nuance: 아저씨 is a native word for a middle-aged or grown man, and it does double duty as a friendly way to flag down a male stranger — a shopkeeper, a taxi driver, a delivery man — much like English 'mister' or 'sir', but warmer and more casual. The cultural pitfall for English speakers is age sensitivity: because 아저씨 implies 'middle-aged', calling a man in his twenties or early thirties 아저씨 can sting, since you're effectively saying he looks past his youth; for a younger-looking man people hedge with 저기요 ('excuse me') or 선생님. Its female counterpart is 아주머니 (and casual 아줌마), and the younger-male equivalents are 오빠/형 (for someone close) or 청년 in formal description. It ends in a vowel, so it takes 예요 and 가 (아저씨예요, 아저씨가). Note that 아저씨 is informal — in a business or polite setting you'd upgrade to 선생님 or 사장님 rather than 아저씨.

usage: a person living nearby; also neighbors collectively
noun + 이에요 after the final consonant ㅅ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
옆집 (the house next door) + 이웃; cf. 이웃 사람 (a neighbor)
examples: 우리 이웃은 아주 친절해요.
Our neighbor is very kind.
이웃 + 은 as topic; can be one person or 'the neighbors'
이웃이 떡을 나눠 줬어요.
A neighbor shared rice cakes with us.

저는 옆집 이웃과 사이가 좋아요.
I get along well with my next-door neighbor.
real situation: 이웃과 = 'with the neighbor', 사이가 좋다 idiom
nuance: 이웃 is a native word (no hanja) for a neighbor — someone who lives close by — and it flexibly means either one specific neighbor or neighbors as a group, depending on context: 좋은 이웃 (a good neighbor), 이웃 사람 (the people next door), 이웃 나라 (a neighboring country). First, pronunciation: the final ㅅ is unreleased and sounds like a ㄷ-stop when alone (이웃 ≈ '이욷'), but before a vowel-initial particle it links and softens, so 이웃이 comes out like '이우시' and 이웃을 like '이우슬' — getting this liaison right is what makes it sound natural. Second, it ends in a consonant, so it takes 이에요 and 이 (이웃이에요, 이웃이), not 예요. Culturally, the phrase 이웃사촌 ('a neighbor as close as a cousin') captures how a good 이웃 is valued, and greeting your 옆집 (next door) when you move in is a normal courtesy.
